fatal_errors: The proposed Hf-to-V substitution does not reconstruct the tested intervention: addition of 4.2 at.% Cr and formation of approximately 4 vol.% reticulated Laves phase.

The cited evidence does not demonstrate that partial V substitution reduces density by at least 5% while preserving HfMoTaTiZr strength; it only establishes broad composition-property trends in other RHEAs.
The density prediction is based on atomic mass alone and neglects the substantial molar-volume and lattice contraction expected when replacing large Hf atoms with much smaller V atoms.
The experiment compares tensile results against baseline strengths reported primarily from compression testing, so the proposed 10% retention criterion is not an equivalent comparison.
No quantitative fracture-strain or toughness retention threshold is supplied despite preservation of room-temperature mechanical performance being central to the problem.
explanation: The response recognizes the density-strength trade-off and proposes a controlled composition series with numerical density and strength rejection criteria. However, it misses the target intervention, structural mediator, and mechanism. The hidden result depends on dilute Cr addition producing an interconnected Cr2(Ti,Zr,Hf,Ta) Laves network, together with lattice contraction and solid-solution hardening, yielding 1750.6 MPa and 14.0% fracture strain in room-temperature compression. The generated hypothesis instead assumes an unverified single-phase BCC V-substituted alloy and predicts retained strength at 1000 °C without supporting evidence. Its experiment is partly falsifiable, but uses a loading mode inconsistent with the baseline and does not discriminate solid-solution hardening from secondary-phase effects. Moreover, declaring the whole hypothesis falsified if any one of the 20–30% substitutions fails is unnecessarily strong when another substitution level could satisfy the stated intervention.
